question: What is the primary purpose of taking a patient drug history?

options.A: To establish a baseline record of all substances currently or recently used by the patient
options.B: To calculate the patient's exact daily caloric and nutritional requirements
options.C: To evaluate the patient's long-term employment history and occupational risks
options.D: To determine the exact financial cost of the patient's ongoing medical treatment

explanation: A complete drug history provides healthcare providers with an accurate inventory of every substance entering the patient's body to guide safe clinical decisions. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why is relying solely on hospital prescription charts insufficient for a complete drug history?

options.A: Patients frequently memorize hospital charts and alter their home doses accordingly
options.B: Hospital charts are legally required to be destroyed immediately after patient discharge
options.C: Doctors rarely update prescription charts during routine ward rounds in Nigerian hospitals
options.D: Hospital charts exclude over-the-counter remedies, herbal preparations, and self-prescribed medications

explanation: Inpatient records only reflect what is ordered inside the facility, missing the full spectrum of self-administered substances the patient uses outside the hospital. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which detail is essential when recording a patient's prescription medication?

options.A: Exact dose, route, and frequency of administration
options.B: The specific pharmacy where the drug was purchased
options.C: The exact date the pharmaceutical license was issued
options.D: The name of the manufacturing pharmaceutical company

explanation: Knowing how much, how often, and by what route a drug is taken determines its therapeutic effect and safety profile. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h2)

question: Why must a nurse document the exact nature of a previous reaction rather than just noting 'allergy'?

options.A: To comply with pharmaceutical marketing regulations set by national drug agencies
options.B: To ensure the hospital pharmacy can bill the correct insurance provider for treatment
options.C: To prevent the patient from purchasing similar medications at local retail pharmacies
options.D: To distinguish between a mild, manageable side effect and a life-threatening anaphylactic reaction

explanation: Labeling a minor upset stomach as an allergy may unnecessarily restrict a patient from receiving vital therapeutic agents in the future. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h2)

question: What is the primary feature of the 'brown bag' method in medication reconciliation?

options.A: Collecting expired hospital supplies for safe disposal by the environmental unit
options.B: Dispensing weekly doses of chronic medications into labeled paper envelopes
options.C: Storing emergency resuscitation drugs inside a specialized portable canvas pouch
options.D: Having the patient bring all their physical medication containers to the clinical visit

explanation: Physical inspection of actual medicine packages eliminates recall bias and reveals exact strengths and remaining quantities. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h3)

question: A patient with hypertension responds with 'yes' when asked if they take their pills. Which interview technique should the nurse use next to gather deeper clinical data?

options.A: Ask the patient to describe the physical appearance of the pills and how many they swallow daily
options.B: End the medication assessment immediately and assume full compliance with therapy
options.C: Consult the hospital physician to prescribe a completely new set of antihypertensive drugs
options.D: Threaten to withhold further clinic appointments if the patient cannot recall the drug names

explanation: Probing questions help uncover vague answers and clarify whether the patient actually understands and follows their regimen. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h3)

question: Why do many patients omit herbal remedies when asked about their medications?

options.A: They do not consider natural or traditional preparations to be real medical drugs
options.B: Traditional remedies are chemically identical to standard prescription tablets
options.C: Herbal preparations dissolve completely in the body and leave no physical trace
options.D: Federal health regulations strictly prohibit discussing herbal medicine in hospitals

explanation: Cultural perceptions often separate natural supplements from orthodox pharmaceuticals, leading patients to leave them out of standard medication lists unless specifically prompted. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h4)

question: What is a major clinical risk associated with concurrent use of herbal remedies and prescription anticoagulants?

options.A: Instantaneous allergic shock within minutes of oral ingestion
options.B: Immediate crystallization of the renal tubules causing permanent kidney shutdown
options.C: Potentiation or inhibition of drug effects, leading to bleeding risks or therapeutic failure
options.D: Total destruction of normal intestinal flora leading to chronic malabsorption

explanation: Active botanical constituents frequently interact with hepatic enzymes or clotting pathways, altering the expected clinical action of prescribed drugs. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h4)

question: Which factor is a common economic barrier to medication adherence in many Nigerian clinical settings?

options.A: Excessive availability of free government pharmacies
options.B: Universal health insurance covering all prescription items
options.C: Mandatory daily registration fees at public clinics
options.D: Out-of-pocket payment costs for purchasing drugs

explanation: Where comprehensive health insurance coverage is limited, patients frequently ration medications due to personal financial constraints. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h5)

question: How does framing a non-adherence question in a non-judgmental way affect the clinical interview?

options.A: It eliminates the need to perform physical laboratory investigations during admission
options.B: It guarantees that the patient will never experience adverse drug side effects again
options.C: It encourages the patient to give an honest report of their actual medication-taking habits
options.D: It legally binds the hospital to provide all future prescription drugs completely free of charge

explanation: Patients hide non-adherence when they fear scolding or judgment from healthcare providers; normalizing the struggle promotes clinical honesty. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h5)

question: What immediate action should a nurse take upon discovering a discrepancy between a patient's home medication list and the inpatient admission order?

options.A: Administer both sets of medications simultaneously to ensure maximum therapeutic coverage
options.B: Clarify the discrepancy with the attending medical officer before administering any medication
options.C: Discard the inpatient order sheet and follow only what the patient remembers from home
options.D: Document the error in the nursing notes and take no further clinical action

explanation: Safety protocols require resolving conflicting medication orders with the prescriber before drug administration to prevent overdose or adverse events. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h6)

question: Why is structured documentation of a drug history vital during interprofessional shift handovers?

options.A: It replaces the need for verbal communication between incoming and outgoing nursing staff
options.B: It serves as a legal advertisement for pharmaceutical companies supplying the ward
options.C: It prevents critical medication data from being lost and ensures safe continuity of care across shifts
options.D: It allows the administrative billing department to calculate final hospital utility charges

explanation: Clear written records maintain clinical continuity, ensuring incoming nurses are fully aware of active drug therapy and special precautions. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h6)
